note: Extracted from SRC-017 (ICH Q7, Step 4, 2000), sections 10.2, 17.4 and 17.6 (printed pages; file page minus 6), with one reading from SRC-006 (Grant, 2002), chapter 4, printed p. 283. ICH Q7 states general expectations for transporting APIs and intermediates; it gives no temperature ranges, no excursion limits and nothing on finished products. No held source quantifies what a temperature excursion does to any peptide. Those are recorded as gaps rather than filled.

topic.shortDescription: What the held guidance says about moving pharmaceutical ingredients without harming them, and the much larger part it leaves unsaid.
topic.simpleSummary: Between the place a peptide is made and the place it is used, it is stored, packed, handed to couriers and sometimes repackaged. International manufacturing guidance for pharmaceutical ingredients says they should be transported in a way that does not harm their quality, that any special transport or storage conditions should be printed on the label, that the company doing the shipping should know and follow those conditions, and that repackaging should be done carefully enough to avoid mix-ups and contamination. What the Tides Index does not hold is any source that says what a particular temperature, for a particular time, does to a particular peptide. A test result from before shipping cannot tell you what happened during it.
topic.practitionerSummary: ICH Q7 s. 10.21–10.23: APIs and intermediates should be transported so as not to adversely affect quality, special transport or storage conditions should be stated on the label, and the manufacturer should ensure a transport contractor knows and follows them. Section 10.24 requires batch distribution records sufficient for recall. Section 17.4 requires repackaging, relabelling and holding to be performed under appropriate GMP controls to avoid mix-ups and loss of identity or purity, and under environmental conditions that avoid contamination; s. 17.6 requires quality information and the original manufacturer's identity and batch to be passed on. Grant's degradation routes (oxidation, hydrolysis, aspartimide formation) and advice to re-evaluate long-stored material explain why conditions in transit matter chemically, but no held source quantifies excursion effects for any peptide.
topic.whatItProves: That, for pharmaceutical ingredients, transport conditions are part of quality rather than logistics: they are expected to be defined, labelled, communicated to carriers and preserved through repackaging.
topic.whatItDoesNotProve: It does not give any acceptable temperature range or excursion limit, and does not establish what any excursion does to any peptide. It does not apply to finished products or consumer shipments. It does not establish that a pre-shipment certificate describes material after transit.
topic.commonMisinterpretations: That lyophilised peptide is indifferent to transport. The held textbook describes degradation routes for dry material too, including deamidation with residual acid and reactions involving adsorbed solvent; how fast they proceed in a given shipment is not established.

locations.chapter: 17. Agents, Brokers, Traders, Distributors, Repackers, and Relabellers

claims.claimText: ICH Q7 states that APIs and intermediates should be transported in a manner that does not adversely affect their quality, that special transport or storage conditions should be stated on the label, and that the manufacturer should ensure a transport contractor knows and follows the appropriate conditions.
claims.plainLanguageText: For pharmaceutical ingredients, shipping conditions are supposed to be defined, labelled and followed by the carrier.
claims.interpretationNotes: Q7 ss. 10.21–10.23. General expectations only; no conditions are specified.
claims.uncertaintyText: API scope. Q7 gives no numerical transport limits.

evidence.interpretation: Transport without adverse effect on quality; conditions on the label; contractor compliance.

claims.claimText: Under ICH Q7, repackaging, relabelling and holding of APIs and intermediates should be performed under appropriate GMP controls to avoid mix-ups and loss of identity or purity, and repackaging should be carried out under environmental conditions that avoid contamination and cross-contamination.
claims.plainLanguageText: Every time material is opened and repacked, there is a chance of mix-up or contamination, so it is supposed to be controlled.
claims.interpretationNotes: Q7 ss. 17.40–17.41. The repackaging link in the chain.

evidence.interpretation: GMP controls on repackaging and holding to preserve identity and purity.

claims.claimText: Because peptides can degrade over time by known chemical routes, and the textbook recommends re-evaluating long-stored material, a test result obtained before storage and shipment describes the material at the time of testing rather than necessarily after transit.
claims.plainLanguageText: A test done before shipping describes the material before shipping.
claims.interpretationNotes: An interpretation resting on Grant p. 283; the source does not discuss transport explicitly. Recorded as a contextualising reading, not a finding about transport.
claims.uncertaintyText: No held source measures change during transit for any peptide.

evidence.interpretation: Degradation routes and re-evaluation after storage; transport is not addressed directly.

Transport and cold-chain expectations for finished peptide products.
notYetSupported.why: ICH Q7 is limited to APIs and intermediates and gives no numerical conditions.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Good distribution practice guidance for medicinal products.
